en: A short-lived fortified settlement on a narrow headland with massive walls on both landward and seaward sides, dug by Karageorghis in 1979–86. A Bronze Age harbour town that became a Phoenician city around 850 BCE and, from the fifth century, a kingdom whose Phoenician kings were vassals of Persia. Its temple of Astarte was one of the largest in the Phoenician world. The city continued as Larnaca and is the birthplace of the philosopher Zeno the Stoic.

en: A plaque over the entrance dates the Ottoman rebuilding of the fort to 1625, though a Turkish garrison had held the site since 1570 and there was a Lusignan work here before that. It carried the guns that saluted arriving consuls, then served the British as a prison with a gallows into the 1940s, and is now the Larnaca Medieval Museum.

Built over the tomb found in 890 inscribed 'Lazarus, four days dead, friend of Christ'. Taken as a mosque after 1571 and sold back to the Orthodox in 1589, it was then shared with Latin worshippers for about two centuries, an arrangement recorded in Latin graffiti in the walls. Its bell tower went up after the Ottoman reform of 1857 permitted belfries. A fire in 1970 destroyed much of the iconostasis, and in November 1972 human remains were found in a marble sarcophagus under the altar and identified as part of the saint's relics.

Founded after the fall of Enkomi, by legend by Teucer of the Trojan War, Salamis was the leading city-kingdom of Cyprus for most of a millennium. Its kings Evagoras I and Nikokreon dominated the island. After earthquakes in the fourth century it was rebuilt by Constantius II as Constantia and made the capital, until the Arab raids of 647–649 and the sand took it.
